iterations.theme: Childbirth as a joyful event: the personal experience of Andrea Piškor, the role of the companion, informed decisions, the role of the father and the attitude toward the healthcare system

sections.subtitle: A topic that concerns everyone: from pregnancy to early motherhood
sections.screenshot_description: Željka Markić opens the podcast and announces the topic of pregnancy, childbirth and early motherhood
sections.content:
Željka Markić opens the podcast with a topic that is, as she emphasizes, at the same time the most intimate and socially vital. It concerns pregnancy, childbirth and early motherhood, and this topic concerns a large number of women, their husbands and children. Precisely for that reason Markić thinks it should be talked about.

The guest is **Andrea Piškor**, a certified birth educator who helps pregnant women and couples to prepare, to become informed and to feel supported on the path toward childbirth and immediately after it. Piškor is the mother of three boys and one girl, a master of economics and a former teacher. After her own experience of motherhood, including a difficult first birth, she directed her professional path toward education and support of pregnant women and parents.

Today she is the owner of a sole-proprietorship business for instruction. She deals with individual preparations of women, mothers and fathers for pregnancy, childbirth, the period after childbirth and breastfeeding. Markić also reveals how she learned about her: through a close friend whom Piškor helped to prepare well for childbirth, together with her husband. The friend had not even expected that in her environment. The host thanks the guest for finding time for the conversation among numerous obligations, which include the women she accompanies and her own family.

sections.subtitle: From economics and school to a calling: questions that gave no peace
sections.screenshot_description: Andrea Piškor explains how her own birth experience led her to birth education
sections.content:
To the question of how she came from economics and work in school to the calling of birth educator and companion, Andrea Piškor answers simply: with her own experience. She thinks above all of her first birth some fifteen years ago, and then of the experience of motherhood.

Piškor emphasizes that for approximately fifteen years, as long as her motherhood lasts, she has been focused on pregnancy and childbirth. It is an area of her interest that she researched in her free time. For a good ten years she sought answers to the question of whether a birth such as happened to her is the way it should be. As she grew in faith and matured spiritually, the question also imposed itself whether this is God's plan for motherhood: a birth from which a woman emerges wounded, physically and emotionally, hurt on all levels of being, discouraged, sad and abandoned.

Piškor admits that a traumatic experience can happen to anyone. The additional impetus came about because of a social saying that she calls a „slap“: *„Everything is fine as long as you and the baby are alive.“* That attitude, she says, deprived her of peace and encouraged her to research. Markić agrees: not everything is fine, and the minimum is not the maximum. Piškor adds that one wants something more, the joy of motherhood and something in which the mother can enjoy.

sections.subtitle: Childbirth is in its essence a joyful event
sections.screenshot_description: Andrea Piškor explains the role of oxytocin as the hormone of love and joy in childbirth
sections.content:
Piškor emphasizes that every birth is hard and extremely strenuous for the organism, even when it is the fastest and easiest. It touches every component of a woman, emotional, spiritual and physical. But regardless of what the birth is like and how hard it is, there is always joy and fulfillment that must not be taken away. Markić describes this as pride and fulfillment in what the woman has achieved.

Piškor claims that birth is in its essence a joyful event, and for this she cites scientific grounding. Birth begins with **oxytocin**, which drives it forward. She calls it the hormone of love and joy, and it is secreted in very intimate situations, in which the woman feels supported, encouraged and safe.

This message, she emphasizes, is to be carried to all families, not only to women and mothers: motherhood is joyful, birth is not torment and such a birth is not God's plan for motherhood.

Over the years Piškor worked in her profession, but the passion for research accompanied her. After the second birth and third pregnancy, and especially after the third birth, she decided to deal exclusively with what she experiences as her calling. Markić emphasizes that it is great luck to find a job that has meaning and in which a person can grow. She is glad that such support for women exists in Croatia too.

sections.subtitle: The first birth: unprepared and the „slap of the system“
sections.screenshot_description: Andrea Piškor talks about the traumatic experience of her first birth and unpreparedness
sections.content:
To Markić's question of what was difficult in the first birth, Piškor first warns that it is better to speak of a traumatic experience. The perception of birth is different: the same birth can be excellent for one woman, and another can experience it as trauma, so this must not be diminished. The experience is someone else's and should be respected as it is.

Her first birth was also medically difficult. It was long-lasting, and the baby was in a more complicated position, to which she received answers only later. What made it traumatic, however, was what was not the difficulty in itself: Piškor came as an unprepared first-time mother. She prepared by reading a book about a spiritual approach to giving birth and expected conditions such as the author describes. She did not want to listen to others' experiences because, she says, those are mostly told hard stories. A woman who had a difficult birth, she explains, wants to tell it.

She went full of trust and experienced a „slap of the system“ that was not as she had expected. She expected joy, tenderness and respect, and the opposite happened. In addition, a situation also occurred that cannot be influenced: a great crowd in the maternity ward, as well as, as always, a lack of medical staff and general chaos. The combination with a difficult birth resulted in her feeling bad and entering the period after birth, as Markić sums up, „from a minus“.

Piškor says that this experience today helps her understand the women she works with, their hardships and the importance of preparation for birth, that is, of a positive birth experience for everything that follows afterwards.

sections.subtitle: What a companion does: education, being informed and calm decisions
sections.screenshot_description: Andrea Piškor describes the four parts of the preparation program for parents
sections.content:
To the question of what her tasks are as a companion, Piškor answers that she combines two roles. She educates as a birth educator, and then remains available for accompaniment. Her complete preparation program is divided into four parts. Some couples are educated for everything, and some choose individual parts. Most often they decide on education on preparation for birth and breastfeeding, and in addition there is preparation for the period after birth and preparation for pregnancy, that is, for what is usual to expect in pregnancy and how to enjoy it.

The first part is the foundation on which parents get information. Piškor warns that nowadays information is very available, yet people are misinformed and do not know the basics: they do not know what the uterus looks like or where fertilization takes place. If pregnancy was reached without discovering this beauty of God's creation, education is, she says, „the last train“ one can jump onto.

When parents understand what is happening and what the changes are, they are calm at the moment of decision. They have a knowledge base from which they can draw information and agree with each other. Piškor emphasizes that there is no good or bad decision, because every decision is good when it is made together and in peace. Birth cannot be planned in advance. One can have plans and scenarios, but the birth will never be exactly as imagined. Markić adds that one should nevertheless prepare as much as possible, and Piškor concludes that knowing the process brings security, and security enables calm deciding.

sections.subtitle: Available as long as they need her: support without interfering in decisions
sections.screenshot_description: Andrea Piškor talks about the limits of the companion and availability to families
sections.content:
As a companion, Piškor provides support above all to the mother and father, and then to the whole family, whenever they feel the need for it. Very few people stay only at the first part, the education, which she respects. Parents most often contact her in the first month after the baby's birth, when they constantly have questions. She also accompanies them in pregnancy, when the woman herself says she is tired or has a hard day, and when the first labor contractions begin.

Piškor emphasizes that she must know her limits:

- she does not interfere in parents' decisions,
- she does not make decisions in their place,
- she does not negotiate with medical staff in their place,
- she provides above all emotional support, both during pregnancy and during birth, although she is not physically present.

They are in contact very often. While they are talking with Markić, one pregnant woman has just given birth, one was sent home from the maternity ward, and another is expected at any moment. Piškor admits that years of maturing were needed for her to understand that parents themselves set the pace and that it is entirely their right whether to involve her. Her message is: *„I am just here, I support you, everything is fine.“* Often that is exactly what a mother needs to hear: that she is a good mom and is doing the best she knows how.

sections.subtitle: Maternal intuition is not the grandmother's or mother-in-law's
sections.screenshot_description: Željka Markić talks about the importance of the husband's support and leaving decisions to young parents
sections.content:
Markić praises the methodology in which the child's father is included. She thinks that a woman's greatest need is to have the support of the husband and father of her child. She also emphasizes trust in a reasonable, educated woman who takes care of the child and who together with her husband can independently make decisions that are valid.

The host also relates a personal experience with the recent arrival of a grandchild. She and her husband are physicians, so the young people consulted them quite a lot. At one moment she felt the need to say that she knows all sorts of things because she gave birth to and raised four children, and also has a physician's knowledge, but that the mom is someone else. She advised them to gather all information and do what they feel. The older generation, she concludes, must learn to let go.

Piškor adds that she always tells parents that maternal intuition is not the grandmother's, the mother-in-law's or the aunt's, but the mom's. The question is always how the mother feels and what she would want. If she is worried, there is no reason to force staying at home, and one sets off when it is time and when the couple agrees. Nobody should say that a decision is wrong or good. Sometimes a message is enough for a woman: *„I'm thinking of you, I'm praying for you“*, and Piškor sends such a message to women to whom she is a support.

sections.subtitle: Continuity and trust: why to get in touch as early as mid-pregnancy
sections.screenshot_description: Andrea Piškor emphasizes the importance of continuous accompaniment and building a relationship with the family
sections.content:
Markić states that from a person whom Piškor accompanied she heard how much it meant to her to be able to ask questions and to know the answers are expert, and that she gets from the companion what she needs for making a decision.

Piškor emphasizes that continuous accompaniment is key, because nothing can be done in an express fashion. She recommends that parents get in touch at least by the middle of pregnancy. A conversation about birth and other sensitive topics requires trust, and a relationship must first be built. When the relationship is of quality, she says, before the companion is a family that can open up. Numerous friendships have arisen from such relationships.

The companion then knows how the woman feels and what her background story is. Piškor gives examples: a woman may be afraid of birth since conception even though it is her fifth birth, because she had very hard previous experiences. Maybe she has a diagnosis. Maybe in her immediate family she encounters incomprehension of openness to life so she must not complain, but hears: *„Why are you complaining now, whose fault is it?“* Markić adds that women often hear this as an accusation that they themselves are to blame for being pregnant.

Piškor emphasizes that for her it is a great responsibility not to betray the trust parents have given her. She has prepared couples for a third, fourth, fifth and even sixth birth, because every family and every subsequent birth deserve time to be gotten to know. A woman needs to feel respected and that someone truly understands her, and this cannot be faked because it is felt.

sections.subtitle: More than a medical event: spirit, soul and body
sections.screenshot_description: Andrea Piškor talks about birth as an emotional and spiritual event, not only a medical one
sections.content:
Piškor warns that pregnancy and birth are not only medical events, although in the existing system of care they are reduced to exactly that. The doctor is responsible for everything going well, for the woman staying alive and the baby being healthy. Markić calls this the minimum, and Piškor adds that one must look deeper.

The woman should be viewed as a being who has spirit, soul and body, who enters birth spiritually and emotionally. Birth is, she emphasizes, far more emotional than is thought. To be able to enter birth, a woman must secrete oxytocin, and for that she needs a **safe environment**. She must feel trust in the people around her in order to be able to surrender everything to birth so that it flows as it should.

sections.subtitle: Birth is a marathon: let us give it the time it deserves
sections.screenshot_description: Andrea Piškor explains why birth should be given time and how to experience it as a blessing
sections.content:
To Markić's question of what is the greatest obstacle to birth remaining a positive experience, Piškor answers that people are not aware that birth is an event that lasts and needs its time. It is necessary to step back a little from culturally inherited understandings, such as the story of how someone „suffered for two days“. She wonders what two days, or twelve hours, are in an entire life, when a new life is coming.

Piškor invites couples to immerse themselves fully in birth. Through it, she says, they can be blessed as a couple, their marriage can spiritually rise to a new level, and birth need not wound them, but enable them growth and respect for the new life that is coming. She asks why hurry birth and why not allow it to spend half a day at home in light contractions, enjoying and preparing lunch for the older children, with the awareness that birth is coming and that the husband is at home. Such a process can strengthen, bring closer and mature the woman as a mother, the husband as a father, the couple as a married couple and the whole family, regardless of whether it is the first child or the family already exists.

Markić describes such an approach as a way that respects all elements and does not approach birth only technically. She adds that a woman can stay at home longer, understand that birth needs time and not fear it, although nobody likes pain.

sections.subtitle: An over-capacity system and the midwife the pregnant woman does not know
sections.screenshot_description: Andrea Piškor compares the Croatian system with more orderly systems across the border in which the pregnant woman knows her midwife
sections.content:
Markić asks how support for the woman and the way women come to hospitals are harmonized within the healthcare system. Piškor answers that the system of care for pregnant women and women in labor is quite deficient and has much room for improvement. In large systems inertia is great, but positive changes are slowly happening. She thinks change will come from the women giving birth themselves, because if change is not strived for, nothing will happen.

At the same time it must be understood that medical staff are over-capacity and are always lacking. Midwives practically run through the entire shift, so they cannot be blamed for it, but we ask how they will manage to take care of the mother's psychological state and stand by the woman in labor.

Ideally one would have orderly systems such as exist „across the border“. There a pregnant woman gets to know her midwife already in pregnancy and talks with her about what is important to her and her husband. Thus she knows in advance which person will be with her when she comes. In Croatia this role is partly taken over by the companion, but the pregnant woman does not know who will be on duty in the shift. With the renovations of maternity wards it also happened that a woman has to go to a different maternity ward than the one in which she planned to give birth. Because of overbooking there were also cases where a woman is assessed as not yet disposed for the phase of labor and is redirected. Piškor asks how oxytocin will be secreted in such circumstances and how the woman will feel safe when she arrives at the maternity ward, where the doctor has no time even to introduce himself and goes immediately to a vaginal examination. Reason, she says, understands that the examination is necessary, but emotions are something else.

sections.subtitle: Half an hour with the anesthesiologist: informed consent in practice
sections.screenshot_description: Željka Markić describes an example of a conversation with an anesthesiologist before birth in neighboring countries
sections.content:
Markić states that in neighboring countries pregnant women before birth have a conversation not only with the midwife, but also with an **anesthesiologist** about epidural analgesia and about how the woman wants to give birth. That meeting of half an hour, she claims, saves time and money for the healthcare system.

She describes an example in which the doctor explained the options: the woman can decide that she does not want an epidural, and also change her mind during birth. He also added his reasons, saying that if a woman plans to have more children, it would be wise to give birth without an epidural the first time, because the body learns birth, and with an epidural the connection is lost. The woman could thus decide to give birth the first time without it, and at the second or third birth, when she already knows her body, take an epidural. Piškor recognizes this as **informed consent**: the woman received information, was involved in her own birth and was not someone standing on the side.

Piškor adds that in even more orderly systems of care the midwife leads the pregnancy from beginning to end, without going to a gynecologist, except in high-risk pregnancies. The midwife even comes to the home, does a complete examination, answers all the questions and gets to know the family. The companion, who continuously accompanies the family, tries to make up for this gap in our system. She, however, is not of the medical profession and does not have to know the answers to all questions. Women should be directed to seek information in the right places, and not on forums and social networks: a question that is written on a forum after an examination should have been asked of the gynecologist. Parents have the right to information and the duty to take responsibility for their own decisions already in pregnancy.

sections.subtitle: The father at birth: it is enough to be there
sections.screenshot_description: Andrea Piškor explains why the husband's presence at education and birth is key
sections.content:
Piškor emphasizes that her primary calling is not to be at the birth, but to direct the husband to be a support to his wife. She rarely goes with women to the maternity ward. When they ask her whether she would go to the birth, she answers that first the education must be done with the husband present. Very many husbands then decide to be a support to their wives. In society there is still too little talk about fathers: one should talk about moms and dads, and fathers should be empowered.

To the question of what helps women most, Piškor answers that it is the husband's presence at the education. Women sometimes tell her to somehow convey to the husband what his role is. Husbands often think that at birth they must do something excessively important and clever, so when they realize that it is enough just to be there, it is as if a burden falls off them. Piškor encourages men by telling them that they are the father of the child. Ideally there would also be, next to them, an objective person who is not emotionally bound, as an unobtrusive support, but if one has to choose between the companion and the husband or partner, it must always be the father of the child. That way he does not miss the birth of the child and the opportunity for the couple to live it as a special blessing that can raise the marriage and the whole family to a new level.

Markić emphasizes that the husband sees the woman in a completely different light. She mentions that some women said they did not want their husband to see them in that situation, and husbands would say that they have no place there. Piškor thinks that society has moved far away from that idea: in fifteen years of intensive accompaniment she sees a change toward a nicer birth for the woman and the child.

sections.subtitle: Birth plan: a simple conversation of husband and wife
sections.screenshot_description: Andrea Piškor explains what a birth plan looks like and how a couple makes it
sections.content:
To the question of what the birth plan she prepares with the woman looks like, Piškor answers that it can, but need not be a written document. She likes to simplify things, which men especially appreciate. After the education the couple knows the information: what birth consists of, what its phases are, how contractions look and change and what physiological birth looks like. They have also heard what the conditions are in Croatian maternity wards.

Then the husband and wife agree, once or several times, over coffee, about what they want and whether there is a gap between what they would wish and what is possible in the maternity ward. Piškor warns that she is often asked questions such as: „Is an epidural good for me?“ She cannot know whether it is good for someone, and the woman does not know it in advance either, because it depends on what phase of labor she will be in. It is important to understand what an intervention is, what its side effects are and whether the benefit is greater than the current state.

sections.subtitle: Episiotomy and interventions: the problem is not the procedure, but non-involvement
sections.screenshot_description: Andrea Piškor and Željka Markić talk about routine interventions and episiotomy
sections.content:
Piškor emphasizes that interventions are useful and that one should be thankful they exist. They are not useful when they are routine, without medical justification, because then a cascade of intervention after intervention spins. When an intervention has a reason, it should be seen as an advantage. Even an episiotomy, which is frightening to all women, can happen for a justified reason, and the woman can still have a positive birth experience if she understood the procedure, if it was explained to her and if she made the decision.

Piškor claims that the greatest traumas happen when the woman is not involved in the decision-making. The woman, she says, does not have a problem with the intervention, but with the way it was carried out, often without being told what is being done. She cites the example of a woman who only later realized that her amniotic sac had been punctured. Ideally the doctor would say: *„This is my proposal, we can also not do it“*, and the decision would be the woman's. In the maternity ward there is often hurry and a lack of staff, but when the woman is informed and involved, the birth experience is far more positive.

Markić cites statistics according to which France has the lowest rate of episiotomies, about eight percent, while Croatia is somewhere at the level of Germany and Austria, about 20 percent. She thinks that this is the result of a decision of the profession which, according to research, concluded that the consequences that episiotomy is meant to prevent occur in a much smaller percentage of cases. Piškor remarks that many studies show that episiotomy in most cases has no benefit, and the same applies to other interventions. Practices in Croatian maternity wards are not uniform even at the level of one maternity ward, but depend on who the doctor on duty is. Piškor cites an example that an episiotomy is performed routinely even on a woman who came for a fourth birth and had previously given birth vaginally to twins. Markić warns of the consequences: difficult movement and breastfeeding and longer recovery, and even additional burden on the healthcare system.

sections.subtitle: A stressful job: doctors, midwives and companions as allies
sections.screenshot_description: Željka Markić and Andrea Piškor talk about the burden on doctors and the importance of cooperation with the companion
sections.content:
Piškor emphasizes that medical workers do best what they know: preserve the health and life of the child and the woman in labor. They do not have the capacity or the possibilities for care in which the woman would be in the entire focus. Markić adds that the work of gynecologists and midwives is extremely stressful: a healthy woman comes carrying a healthy child, and it is expected that she will also leave healthy with the child in her arms, but a series of situations happens. It is the responsibility of the system that a male doctor and a female doctor can normally go about their day.

Piškor thinks that the head of the delivery room must have good managerial skills, and the greatest stress of his job is the bell which in a shift can ring several times, when for example „13 or 33“ rings and everything must be arranged. Understanding for one another is needed.

She considers the cooperation of the companion, gynecologist and midwives inevitable, so that the family and the mother are in focus. It is a misconception that the story ends with birth: it is only the beginning. A mother who was respected and who feels good emotionally and physically after birth is at a much lower risk of **postpartum depression**. The same holds for a mother who has the support of her husband, a companion or some third person. Such a mother will recover faster and enjoy motherhood, while the birth experience often „steals“ the early joy of motherhood and parenthood.

sections.subtitle: A realistic approach: use the system and do not lie down during birth
sections.screenshot_description: Andrea Piškor talks about positions in labor and the recommendations of the World Health Organization
sections.content:
Markić likes Piškor's realistic approach: the system is as it is and within it one should do the best one can, with the husband beside oneself and an understanding of birth. Piškor agrees that the doctor is needed and that one should give birth in the delivery room. She is convinced that the lying position is not the best for giving birth and that it should be avoided. She recalls a document of the World Health Organization, which as an approximate date she ties to 1999, with a recommendation that the woman in labor be encouraged not to lie during birth, but to be active on her feet and in the position she wants. There are, she adds, many reasons why this is so. She is convinced that doctors and midwives themselves sometimes know that it would be better otherwise, but are where they are.

Because of this, cooperation with the companion is important, so that the woman is covered completely: spirit, soul and body. Markić cites the example of a tub with warm water in the maternity ward. The tub can help for several reasons, including easier bearing of contractions, and the woman does not have to give birth in it, but can stay for some time. But it happens that a hospital has a tub and nobody offers women to use it, or that births in it are not performed at all. Piškor adds that medical staff cannot be blamed: when it is already complicated enough, why complicate even more, especially when the midwife runs the whole shift. Markić concludes that the system should provide these people with time: the midwife time for the woman, the gynecologist appointments for conversation with women in labor, and the anesthesiologist for explaining and meeting. Such preparation would better prepare the woman for birth and reduce later burden on the system.
keywords: time for the woman in labor

sections.subtitle: Open days and differences among doctors
sections.screenshot_description: Andrea Piškor talks about maternity ward open days and unequal practice among shifts
sections.content:
Piškor states that some maternity wards throughout Croatia have started organizing **open days**, once a month or more often, when pregnant women and partners go through a workshop and look around the maternity ward. She thinks, however, that often it remains only at that: the space is learned and information received, but when birth comes, a different female or male doctor is on shift and the rules that were mentioned no longer apply.

On the basis of work experience she concludes that rules do not exist even at the level of one maternity ward, but often the individual decides. That is her personal conclusion from experience, and she repeats it as a reason why an informed and involved woman remains key.

sections.subtitle: When birth happens outside the hospital: parents' calm most important
sections.screenshot_description: Andrea Piškor tells about unplanned births at home and the importance of parents' calm
sections.content:
Markić asks whether Piškor has had cases of women giving birth unplanned outside the hospital. Piškor answers that parents always prepare for birth as a process: *„birth is a marathon, not a sprint“*, so it needs to be given the time it deserves. Still, there are also „movie scenarios“. They do not happen often, but she says she would not have believed they are possible if she did not do this job. Still, there are a few per year.

Piškor retells one case: the husband and wife set off toward the maternity ward, and in the garage the woman said she does not want to give birth in the garage, that she wants to go back up because it is winter and she will soon give birth. She barely got back to the apartment, and the husband immediately called the Emergency Medical Service. Markić comments that the woman made the decision because she realized that in the garage it is cold and dirty. Piškor cites other examples: a woman goes to the bathroom and birth begins, and another gets in touch with a message that she has just given birth in the bathroom and that they are waiting for the Emergency Medical Service. In such cases it is often women who have already given birth and know what contractions are.

Markić concludes that this shows how important preparation is, not only of mothers but also of fathers. Piškor emphasizes that the most important thing is that parents are **calm**. When they ask what they need, she answers that they do not need to know everything, and she herself is not a doctor and does not believe in the lie that she must know and say everything. When parents are calm and secure with each other and when the process is familiar to them, everything, she says, is fine.

iterations.theme: Breastfeeding and early motherhood: difficulties, knowledge and support, closing message and contact

sections.subtitle: Breastfeeding is not only instinct: a skill that is learned and prepared already in pregnancy
sections.screenshot_description: Andrea Piškor explains that breastfeeding is natural, but also a skill that is learned and perfected
sections.content:
Željka Markić continues the conversation about childbirth with a question about the period after it. She recalls that Andrea Piškor helps women also in establishing breastfeeding and adds that this too is a demanding task.

Andrea Piškor explains that her work includes preparation for breastfeeding already in pregnancy. Breastfeeding is, she says, **the most natural way of feeding** because humans are mammals. Still, she warns that there are difficulties, so she always tells her mothers that breastfeeding is **a skill that is learned and perfected**. This holds also for women who carry negative impressions from earlier experience. Initial problems, she notes, can happen, and she is then at the mothers' disposal.

As an example she cites a pregnant woman who contacted her while she was driving to the studio. The woman had given birth the previous night and reported that everything was fine, with a slightly poorer latch of the baby on the breast. The problem, says Andrea Piškor, they solved quickly together. She concludes that the greatest problem is precisely the lack of knowledge.

sections.subtitle: A generation that has not seen breastfeeding: how knowledge was lost and why misconceptions prevail
sections.screenshot_description: Andrea Piškor talks about the generation gap and lost knowledge about breastfeeding
sections.content:
Andrea Piškor emphasizes that today's generations of mothers **did not grow up alongside women who breastfeed**. Many breastfed for the first time without ever before having seen a woman breastfeeding. Breastfeeding was, according to her words, long suppressed, and in the last ten years or so marketing campaigns for breastfeeding started. Knowledge about how breastfeeding actually functions was lost along the way.

The consequence is misconceptions that she cites as questions mothers ask:

- how is it possible that the breasts will not produce enough milk,
- how is it possible that the milk is not good or strong enough.

Andrea Piškor answers that the human species was created so as to sustain itself by breastfeeding. If there were so many problems, she says, people would have died out long ago. Therefore **every mom can breastfeed her child**, just as she can give birth, because she was created that way.

Željka Markić asks about cases with medical obstacles. Andrea Piškor confirms that diagnoses and pathologies exist, but emphasizes that she is speaking in general, about approximately 90 percent of the population: a healthy mom and a healthy baby, with an uneventful birth. She also warns about stereotypes that can discourage the mother already in the maternity ward, such as messages that she has small breasts and will not be able to breastfeed or that she will need "hats". The mother then, she says, is immediately and automatically discouraged.

sections.subtitle: The law of supply and demand: what awaits a mother who on the third day after a cesarean section waits for milk
sections.screenshot_description: Andrea Piškor as an economist explains breastfeeding through the law of supply and demand
sections.content:
Andrea Piškor, who is an economist by profession, claims that breastfeeding functions on **the law of supply and demand**. She considers this a phenomenal comparison that helps mothers understand the process.

Mothers who gave birth by cesarean section often contact her. They prepare for this in advance, when it is known the birth will be by cesarean section, because a mother can successfully breastfeed also after a cesarean section. Still, she describes a typical call: a mother on the third day after a cesarean section reports that she is waiting for her milk to come in. To the question of what she does while waiting, she answers that – she waits. Andrea Piškor then tells her that they could wait like that until the birthday. Nothing will happen by waiting.

Željka Markić asks her to explain that, and Andrea Piškor answers that **milk is made when the baby breastfeeds**. Therefore it is key to know how breastfeeding functions, instead of passively waiting for the milk to "come by itself".

sections.subtitle: "Why is he breastfeeding again?": half of breastfeeding is not hunger, but a need for security
sections.screenshot_description: Andrea Piškor explains non-nutritive breastfeeding and the baby's need for the mother's closeness
sections.content:
Andrea Piškor explains that the baby instinctively wants to be at the breast because it is pleasant for her and the innate instinct of sucking. She emphasizes that in the first days in the maternity ward, and later too, throughout the entire first year of life, **the nutritional need for food is not always the reason for breastfeeding**. She estimates that approximately **50 percent of breastfeeding is non-nutritive**, that is, that the child wants to be at the breast for comfort and security.

The physiological needs of the baby are to be fed, full, put to sleep and changed, but also safe. And safe is, says Andrea Piškor, only with mom at the breast. The surroundings often interpret this wrongly with questions such as "why is he breastfeeding again, he has just eaten" or with the claim that the mother has "weak milk". In fact breastfeeding is established precisely like this: the baby has a natural need to be with mom, and sucking calms her.

That is, she adds, needed also by the mother. Thereby her brain "realizes" that it is entering the process of lactation and that it must produce milk. Neither waiting nor **the most expensive tea for nursing mothers** can stimulate that. The mother needs to eat and drink well, but milk comes from the baby, when she is put to the breast and starts to breastfeed.

Željka Markić also notes that this is a lot of work.

sections.subtitle: Fullness of the breasts between the third and fifth day: an expected difficulty that need not be panic
sections.screenshot_description: Andrea Piškor explains physiological breast fullness and how to stay calm
sections.content:
Andrea Piškor repeats that breastfeeding is natural, but often brings difficulties, and many of them stem from **social expectations**, such as the question of why the baby is breastfeeding again. Some difficulties, she emphasizes, are completely expected.

It is very probable, she says, that the mother in the group of about 90 percent will experience **physiological fullness of the breasts between the third and fifth day**. The breasts then suddenly become full, warm and hard. A mother who does not know this can panic or not notice it and do nothing for three days, and then she is very close to mastitis. A mother who knows this is a normal process, and what to do at that moment, stays calm.

Andrea Piškor repeats that **the joy of motherhood must not be stolen**. The period is extremely turbulent and demanding for both parents and the whole family, but the baby is so small only for the first month, which is very precious time. She tells parents that insecurity and a lack of information must not steal the joy of early parenthood from them.

Željka Markić connects this with babies' crying. When someone warns you that a baby's crying is tiring however much you love her, it is easier to bear it and to understand that there is nothing strange in it. Andrea Piškor agrees: when situations are familiar, parents are calm.

sections.subtitle: A vulnerable mother after birth: listen before anything is said
sections.screenshot_description: Andrea Piškor talks about the mother's vulnerability after birth and caution when advising
sections.content:
Andrea Piškor emphasizes that in the postpartum period it is important to know that difficulties happen to everyone. About this, she says, people just do not talk. Željka Markić adds that because of silence women easily think they are doing something wrong.

The mother is in this period **extremely vulnerable**, and every piece of information she hears can sound to her like a message: "I'm not good enough, I'm not doing well." Even the best-intended criticism requires caution and gentleness. Andrea Piškor advises that one should first hear out what the mother has to say, before anything is said, and to think five times about how to say it.

An example she cites: a guest comes and says that it is perhaps too warm in the apartment. The mother can afterwards repeat that sentence a hundred times in her head and wonder what kind of parents she and her partner are if they heated the apartment too much. Andrea Piškor describes a mother who receives advice such as "you must cover him" or "he is hot" as a person in "total system breakdown".

A woman needs someone to **carefully listen** to her and to believe her. Željka Markić adds that things should be said to her in a way that she can hear, and recalls that it is the mom who has **maternal intuition** and who actually knows all this.

sections.subtitle: The most important message to pregnant women: birth is a physiological process and in its essence joy
sections.screenshot_description: Andrea Piškor tells pregnant women that birth is a joyful event, not a source of fear
sections.content:
Željka Markić asks Andrea Piškor which one thing a pregnant woman should learn in time. Andrea Piškor answers that it is the realization that **birth is a physiological process**. It happens every day, and many women enter birth and give birth daily. This is, she emphasizes, something joyful: birth is in its essence joy.

She repeats a thought she always says: **"Fear is afraid of love."** God's plan for motherhood, she says, is not fear. She recalls that every woman, when she remembers her birth, had a joyful beginning, when it began and when something signaled that the baby would arrive.

Andrea Piškor invites that time and importance be devoted to birth, instead of wishing it to end as soon as possible. She clarifies that by this she does not mean that a woman should suffer, because intense contractions last toward the end of the birth, and Željka Markić as a mother herself knows what it is about. Still, birth should be given a form of beauty, the time and space it deserves, and one should go through it with joy and welcome the child.

sections.subtitle: How to reach Andrea Piškor: recommendations, website and social networks
sections.screenshot_description: Željka Markić asks Andrea Piškor how women can contact her
sections.content:
At the end of the conversation Željka Markić thanks the guest and says she is glad that women have the opportunity to have her support. Then she asks how one can reach her and whether she has a website.

Andrea Piškor answers that she has a **website** that deals with supporting parents in early parenthood, as well as **Instagram**, and also mentions a Facebook page. Still, experience has shown her that people most often come to her **by recommendation**. Željka Markić confirms that she herself heard about her through a friend. Andrea Piškor explains that behind her work stand relationships of trust that remain.

Željka Markić concludes the conversation with thanks to Andrea Piškor and addresses the viewers, hoping that the conversation was as interesting to them as it was to her, and bids them farewell until the next occasion.
